questions.q: Why can gradients 'explode' in deep or recurrent networks?
options: Because PyTorch caps the number of parameters allowed
Because the chain rule multiplies many terms together, and if those terms run slightly above 1, the product can grow exponentially with depth
Because the dataset was shuffled incorrectly
Because dropout was left enabled during evaluation
questions.explain: Gradients are products of many chain-rule terms. If those terms are consistently somewhat larger than 1, the product compounds and can grow exponentially with network depth or sequence length.

questions.q: In the training step `loss.backward(); torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0); optimizer.step()`, where does clipping happen relative to the other calls?
options: Before loss.backward(), so gradients are never computed in full
After backward() has populated gradients, and before optimizer.step() consumes them
After optimizer.step(), to undo an already-applied update
Inside the loss function itself
questions.explain: Clipping needs populated .grad values to act on, so it runs after loss.backward() and before optimizer.step() uses those gradients to update the weights.

questions.q: What does `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_` do to the gradients when the combined norm exceeds `max_norm`?
options: It sets every gradient to zero
It rescales every gradient proportionally so the new combined norm equals max_norm, preserving direction
It randomly drops some gradients
It increases the learning rate to compensate
questions.explain: clip_grad_norm_ rescales all gradients by the same proportional factor so the resulting combined norm equals max_norm — the gradient's direction is unchanged, only its magnitude shrinks.

options: clip_grad_value_ clamps each gradient element independently to a fixed range, which can change the gradient's direction; clip_grad_norm_ rescales proportionally and preserves direction
They are two names for the exact same function
clip_grad_value_ only works with the Adam optimizer
clip_grad_value_ clips the learning rate instead of the gradient
questions.explain: clip_grad_value_ clamps each gradient component to [-clip_value, clip_value] independently, which can distort the gradient's direction, unlike the proportional, direction-preserving rescaling of clip_grad_norm_.

questions.q: You notice occasional sharp spikes in your training loss that don't correspond to anything unusual in the data. What is a reasonable, low-risk thing to try first, based on this lesson?
options: Immediately redesign the entire model architecture
Add gradient clipping with a max_norm around 1.0-5.0
Delete the validation set
Switch every layer to nn.Dropout
questions.explain: Occasional unexplained loss spikes are a classic symptom of exploding gradients, and gradient clipping with a modest max_norm is a cheap, low-risk mitigation to try before more invasive changes.
